0.title: Wealth, Generosity, and the Kingdom of God
0.overview:
Jesus talked about money more than almost any other subject. In the Gospels, roughly one in seven of his statements touches on wealth, possessions, or economic relationships. This is not because he was preoccupied with finance but because he understood the heart -- and money is one of the most reliable diagnostics of the heart. 'For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also' (Matt. 6:21). Show me what you spend and you've told me what you love.

The Christian church has always struggled with money -- not because money is evil (it isn't; 1 Tim. 6:17 says God 'richly provides us with everything to enjoy'), but because the love of money is 'a root of all kinds of evil' (1 Tim. 6:10). The problem is not wealth; it is disordered desire for wealth. And in a consumer culture that insistently defines life by acquisition and comfort, this disordering is both universal and invisible. We absorb its assumptions without noticing, and our relationship to money often looks more like the world than the kingdom.

This study is not a financial planning course. It is a theological and pastoral examination of what the Bible says about wealth, simplicity, contentment, generosity, and stewardship. We will consider money as a gift to be received with gratitude, a test to be faced with integrity, a tool to be deployed for the kingdom, and a danger to be resisted with vigilance. The goal is not guilt but freedom -- the freedom of the person who has heard Jesus say 'You cannot serve God and money' (Matt. 6:24) and has chosen to serve God.

Key voices in this study: Tim Keller's 'Generous Justice' and 'Every Good Endeavor', John Piper's 'Desiring God' and 'Battling Unbelief', Randy Alcorn's 'The Treasure Principle', R.C. Sproul on stewardship, Craig Blomberg's 'Neither Poverty nor Riches', and the great tradition of Reformed thought on vocation, creation, and the cultural mandate.

1.title: Money as Gift: Created Goodness and the Danger of Idolatry
1.overview:
The first thing Scripture says about the material world is that it is good (Gen. 1:31). God created the physical order -- including the potential for wealth -- and declared it very good. This matters enormously for a Christian theology of money, because it rules out the error of treating wealth as inherently corrupt or the physical world as a prison to escape. Creation is good. Work is good. Economic exchange is good. The capacity to earn, save, invest, and give is a gift from the Creator to his image-bearers.

And yet the fall has profoundly distorted the human relationship to material goods. What was meant to be received as a gift from a good Father has become, for fallen humanity, a source of security, identity, and ultimate meaning. We look to wealth for what only God can give: safety, significance, and sufficiency. This is idolatry -- not because we have money, but because money has us. The idol is not the money itself but the trust we place in it, the identity we derive from it, the comfort we demand from it.

Keller's insight is sharp: every human being has something that functions as their 'righteousness' -- the thing that makes them feel worthy and significant. For many in the modern West, that thing is financial security. When it is threatened, we panic. When it is achieved, we feel we can finally breathe. The gospel confronts this not with poverty but with a different kind of wealth: 'For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich' (2 Cor. 8:9). The riches of Christ make us free to hold money loosely.
1.theology: The doctrine of creation establishes money as a gift; the doctrine of providence maintains it as held in God's hands; the doctrine of sin explains why we worship it; and the doctrine of redemption sets us free from it. The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 27) teaches that God is 'upholding and governing heaven and earth and all creatures' by his providential hand -- which means that wealth comes and goes by his sovereign purpose, not by our achievement alone. This is both humbling (we did not earn it alone) and liberating (we do not need to clutch it). The Puritan William Perkins taught that all callings are God's callings, and all honest labor produces wealth for God's purposes -- including the purposes of generosity to others.
1.examples: A successful entrepreneur sits in a Bible study and hears for the first time that God gave him both his talent and the opportunity to use it -- that his success is not a vindication of his superior effort but a gift from a generous God (Deut. 8:17-18: 'You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth'). Something shifts. He stops thinking of his company as his achievement and begins thinking of it as his stewardship. The decisions that follow -- about giving, about how he treats employees, about business practices -- look different under that lens. The gift received with gratitude is always used more wisely than the achievement clutched as a possession.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's definition of 'great gain' is deliberately subversive: it is contentment, not accumulation. The logic is simple and devastating: we arrived with nothing and we will leave with nothing, so the game of acquisition is ultimately played with borrowed chips. Contentment is not the absence of desire; it is the presence of enough -- and 'enough' is defined not by the market but by the God who has promised to supply all our needs according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Phil. 4:19). Godliness with contentment is great gain: it is the wealth that cannot be taken.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The danger for the wealthy is not their wealth but their hope. Paul does not say 'tell the rich to give everything away.' He says 'tell them not to set their hopes on their riches.' Wealth is uncertain -- market crashes, illness, death, inflation -- and to rest your hope on something uncertain is to be perpetually anxious. But 'God who richly provides everything to enjoy' is the alternative. He is the source; wealth is the channel. When the channel becomes the source, idolatry has arrived. When the source is trusted, the channel can be used with joy and given away with freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the great warning for every prosperous season: the temptation to self-congratulation, to the story that goes 'I worked hard, I was smart, I succeeded.' Deuteronomy shatters that story. The very capacity to work, the intelligence to succeed, the health to persist, the opportunities that opened -- all of it is gift. 'He who gives you power to get wealth.' This does not make effort irrelevant, but it makes pride impossible. Gratitude is the only rational response to a gift, and gratitude expressed in generosity is the most God-honoring use of wealth.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological foundation of Christian generosity is not obligation but the gospel. Jesus, eternally rich in the glories of the Godhead, became poor -- born in a stable, a refugee in Egypt, dependent on the hospitality of others, dying naked on a cross. He did this so that we might receive the imperishable riches of reconciliation with God, adoption as his children, and an eternal inheritance. When we grasp this -- really grasp it -- the grip that money has on our hearts loosens. You cannot be simultaneously gripped by both the wealth of Christ and the wealth of the world. The gospel is the truest financial advice: invest in Christ, and hold everything else loosely.

2.title: Contentment: The Lost Art of Enough
2.overview:
The Apostle Paul wrote 'I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content' (Phil. 4:11) from prison. This is not the contentment of a man who has everything; it is the contentment of a man who has found that Christ is enough regardless of everything. 'I have learned' -- it was not natural, not automatic. Contentment is a discipline, a learned skill, a virtue formed by practice and grace. In the ancient world, as in our own, it was counter-cultural. The Stoics sought contentment through indifference to circumstances; Paul sought it through Christ's strength flowing into him ('I can do all things through him who strengthens me,' Phil. 4:13).

In a consumer culture, contentment is a radical act. The entire machinery of advertising is designed to produce discontent -- to make us feel that our life is incomplete without the next purchase, the next upgrade, the next experience. Contentment resists this machinery not by turning away from the material world (that is Gnosticism) but by receiving what we have as a gift and finding our deepest satisfaction in Christ rather than in things. Randy Alcorn calls this 'the treasure principle': 'You can't take it with you -- but you can send it ahead.' The person with an eternal perspective on wealth is free to give, free to simplify, free to find that their life does not consist in the abundance of their possessions (Luke 12:15).

This unit explores the theology and practice of contentment: what it means to be satisfied in God, how to resist the comparison trap, how to practice simplicity without legalism, and how the eternal perspective transforms our relationship to the present. The goal is not poverty but freedom -- the freedom that comes when Christ, not comfort, is the centre of our life.
2.theology: The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q&A 147) lists 'discontentment with our own estate' and 'envying or grieving at the good of our neighbor' as sins against the tenth commandment. Discontentment is a sin because it is a failure of faith -- it says, in effect, 'What God has given me is not enough, and he is not enough.' Calvin taught that the fear of poverty is one of the greatest obstacles to generous living, and that it can only be overcome by a deep conviction of God's providence. The fruit of trusting God's provision is the freedom to give away what we have been given -- not because we don't value it, but because we value something more.
2.examples: A family in a middle-class suburb makes a deliberate decision to live on 80% of their income and give away 20% -- not as a mathematical rule but as a regular practice of gratitude. Over five years, they discover something remarkable: they feel richer, not poorer. The discipline of giving has broken the power of accumulation over them, and they have learned to find joy in simpler pleasures. Their children grow up with a different relationship to money than their peers -- not anxious, not acquisitive, but generous. The Puritans had a phrase for this: 'enough is a feast.' Contentment transforms what you have into abundance.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul has been both wealthy (a Pharisee of the Pharisees, educated under Gamaliel) and desperately poor (beaten, shipwrecked, imprisoned, hungry). He claims to have learned contentment in both conditions. This is the proof that contentment is not a function of circumstance but of relationship with Christ. The secret of contentment ('I have learned the secret,' Phil. 4:12) is Christological: 'I can do all things through him who strengthens me' (Phil. 4:13) -- a text that, in context, is not about athletic achievement but about the strength to be content in poverty and the wisdom to hold abundance loosely.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus issues a warning here: 'Take care, and be on your guard.' Covetousness is not a spectacular sin; it is a creeping one. It rarely announces itself. It takes the form of reasonable desires, legitimate ambitions, and understandable comparisons. 'Take care' -- the warning implies that covetousness can take root without our noticing. The counter-statement is the foundation of contentment: life is not defined by possessions. Not enhanced, not completed, not secured by possessions -- it does not consist in them. To believe this is to be free.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The ground of contentment is the presence of God. 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' (from Deut. 31:6, spoken to Joshua as he entered an uncertain future) is the foundation on which contentment rests. If God is always present, then the worst that can happen -- financial ruin, poverty, loss -- cannot deprive us of the best thing: God himself. Contentment is not stoic indifference; it is faith in the abiding presence of the one who is better than anything money can buy.

verseByVerse.quote: But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The famous verse is consistently misquoted: it is not money but the love of money that is the root of evil. Paul traces the problem to desire -- the craving for wealth ('those who desire to be rich') before a single coin has been gained. The desire itself is the snare. And the consequences are severe: 'ruin and destruction,' and 'wandering away from the faith.' The antidote is not asceticism but contentment -- replacing the love of money with the love of God, replacing the craving for wealth with the enjoyment of his gifts.

3.title: Generosity: The Grace of Giving
3.overview:
Generosity is not primarily a financial practice; it is a theological posture. It flows from the character of God himself -- a God who gave the world (John 3:16), who gives wisdom generously to all who ask (James 1:5), who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Tim. 6:17). The most generous act in history was the giving of the Son. All Christian generosity is a response to and a participation in that primordial gift.

The New Testament's most sustained treatment of giving is 2 Corinthians 8-9, where Paul addresses the Corinthians' promised but delayed contribution to the Jerusalem collection. His argument is entirely theological: he doesn't manipulate, he doesn't guilt, he doesn't leverage. He tells the story of the Macedonian churches, who gave 'beyond their means' out of 'abundance of joy' even in 'extreme poverty' (2 Cor. 8:2). Then he points to Jesus: 'For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor' (2 Cor. 8:9). The model for giving is the gospel. And the goal of giving is not merely to meet needs but to produce 'an abundance of thanksgiving to God' (2 Cor. 9:12).

This unit examines the grace of generosity: tithing as a starting point, proportional and cheerful giving as the New Testament standard, giving as an act of worship, giving to the poor as a form of justice, and the remarkable promise that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7) and that the generous person will be enriched in every way (2 Cor. 9:11). The goal is not a pledge card but a transformed heart -- one that has grasped the grace of Christ and responds by extending that grace to others.
3.theology: The Reformed tradition grounds generosity in the doctrine of grace. John Calvin taught that the proper response to the grace of God is gratitude, and gratitude expressed in generosity is one of the primary proofs of genuine faith. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q&A 141) treats 'prodigality' and 'coveting and inordinate prizing and affecting worldly goods' as sins against the eighth commandment, but also lists failure to give to those in need. The Puritans, despite their reputation for frugality, were emphatic about the duty of generous giving -- Richard Baxter's 'Christian Directory' gave extensive guidance on giving proportionally to need and income. Keller summarizes the New Testament standard: give enough that it costs you something, give joyfully not grudgingly, and let the gospel -- not guilt -- be the motive.
3.examples: R.G. LeTourneau, the American construction entrepreneur who eventually gave 90% of his income to Christian missions, said: 'The question is not how much of my money I give to God, but how much of God's money I keep for myself.' He had understood something fundamental: the money was never his. It was entrusted to him. This reframing of ownership transforms giving from sacrifice to stewardship. In a local congregation, a pastor preaches a series on generosity. Afterward, he does not take a pledge. He simply says: 'Go home and pray. Ask God what he wants you to give. Then give that.' The following year, giving to the church increases by 40% -- more than any pledge campaign had ever achieved.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The agricultural metaphor of sowing is important: you give now in order to harvest later, but the harvest is in God's hands and it is often surprising in its form. The harvest of generous giving is not necessarily financial return -- Paul is clear that the enrichment is 'for every good work' (2 Cor. 9:8), not for personal profit. The giver is enriched in every way so that they can be more generous, not more comfortable. And the manner of giving matters as much as the amount: 'not reluctantly or under compulsion.' Cheerful giving is the sign of a heart that has understood the grace it has received.

verseByVerse.quote: ...their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part. ... and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Macedonian churches are the model: extreme poverty + abundance of joy = wealth of generosity. The economics make no sense -- until you factor in that they had 'given themselves first to the Lord.' The sequence is everything. Generosity that does not begin with self-surrender to God is philanthropy, which is admirable but not transforming. Generosity that begins with surrender -- 'Lord, I am yours; all I have is yours' -- produces giving 'beyond their means' that astonishes even the apostle. The gift of the self precedes the gift of money, and makes it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Proverb is not a prosperity-gospel promise; it is a wisdom observation about the paradox of generosity. In God's economy, the closed fist impoverishes and the open hand prospers -- but not necessarily in financial terms. The person who gives freely 'grows all the richer' in the things that matter: in relationship, in peace, in character, in the joy of being used by God. The person who withholds suffers not only material want but the poverty of a closed heart. Generosity is its own reward, even before the harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: He looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box, and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. And he said, 'Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus evaluates giving not by amount but by proportion and sacrifice. The widow's two copper coins -- a day's wages, perhaps, her entire living -- are worth more in God's economy than the large gifts of the wealthy who gave from their surplus. This does not mean large gifts don't matter; they do, and the wealthy have greater capacity for generosity and greater responsibility. But it means that God is watching the heart behind the gift more than the size of the gift. Sacrificial giving is the measure, not absolute amount.

4.title: Justice and the Poor: Money as a Kingdom Tool
4.overview:
The Bible has more to say about the poor than about almost any other subject. There are over 2,000 verses in Scripture that address poverty, wealth, and justice -- more than on prayer and faith combined. This is not because the Bible is primarily a social justice manifesto, but because a God who is perfectly just and perfectly merciful cannot be indifferent to the suffering of the poor. Care for the poor is not an optional extra for the Christian faith; it is a structural requirement of covenant faithfulness.

In the Old Testament, justice for the poor is built into the Mosaic law: gleaning rights for the poor (Lev. 19:9-10), the Year of Jubilee (Lev. 25), the Sabbath year (Deut. 15:1-11), strict prohibitions on exploiting the poor, wages, and lending practices. The prophets thunder against economic injustice with a passion that is almost uncomfortable to read: 'Woe to those who add house to house and join field to field' (Isa. 5:8); 'They sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals' (Amos 2:6). The poor are not merely objects of charity in Scripture; they are image-bearers of God whose dignity demands a response.

In the New Testament, care for the poor is one of the defining marks of the church. The Jerusalem collection that Paul organized was a concrete act of economic solidarity between Gentile and Jewish believers. James is searingly direct: 'Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction' (James 1:27). Keller's 'Generous Justice' makes the argument persuasively: if you have been justified freely by the grace of God, you will be a just person -- justice toward the poor is not a political add-on but a fruit of the gospel.
4.theology: Reformed theology's doctrine of common grace (God's benevolence to all people, regardless of election) provides one foundation for engagement with poverty and justice. But the stronger ground is the imago Dei: every poor person bears the image of God, and to ignore them is to dishonor their Maker. Keller draws on the concept of 'mishpat' (justice) and 'tsedaqah' (righteousness/generosity) from the Hebrew prophets -- the two are always linked in the OT, as if they are two sides of the same coin. A community that does not practice mishpat (fair treatment, equal protection) and tsedaqah (active giving) has not understood the character of God. For the Reformed believer, caring for the poor is not an alternative to the gospel -- it is a fruit of the gospel.
4.examples: William Wilberforce spent 20 years in Parliament fighting for the abolition of the slave trade -- a form of economic injustice so embedded in British wealth creation that many considered it untouchable. He was sustained by his evangelical faith, his friendship with John Newton, and his conviction that the gospel demanded justice for the enslaved. George Muller built orphanages with donated funds, never making his needs publicly known, trusting God to supply -- and God did, consistently, for 60 years. Both men understood that money deployed for the poor is money invested in the kingdom. Today, a congregation plants a food bank, a job-training program, and a financial counseling ministry in a low-income neighborhood. It is not replacing the gospel; it is embodying it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is a startling verse: generosity to the poor is described as lending to God. God himself accepts the loan and promises repayment. This means that giving to the poor is not charity downward but investment upward -- it is a transaction with the Almighty, who is the most reliable debtor in the universe. The poor person is, in some sense, God's representative -- the one in whom God's image is most visibly vulnerable, the one whom God has specially identified himself with (Matt. 25:40: 'As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me').

verseByVerse.quote: There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus... (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The parable of the rich man and Lazarus is not a condemnation of wealth but of indifference. The rich man's sin was not his wealth but his failure to see the man at his gate -- a man with a name (Lazarus -- 'God is my help'), a story, an image-bearing dignity. The gate between them was small. He passed it every day. He never crossed it. The eternal reversal is severe: the one who had everything loses everything; the one who had nothing receives Abraham's bosom. The gospel is not against wealth; it is against the blindness that wealth can produce.

verseByVerse.quote: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him? If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James is relentlessly concrete. Faith that does not meet the physical needs it has the power to meet is dead -- not merely inadequate, but dead. The test case is simple: a brother or sister lacks food and clothing. You have the means to help. You pray for them instead. That is not faith -- that is spiritual evasion. James is not teaching that works save; he is teaching that saving faith works. The works do not earn salvation; they evidence it. A heart genuinely transformed by the grace of Christ will be a generous heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God redefines fasting here: not abstinence from food while maintaining injustice, but active engagement with the poor and oppressed. The religious performance of fasting is worthless if it is not accompanied by the social fruit of justice. This is the prophetic tradition at its sharpest: God is not interested in religious ceremony divorced from moral reality. The worship he accepts is the worship that flows out into justice, generosity, and solidarity with the poor. The tithe given to the church and the food given to the hungry are not separate acts; they are one act of worship.

5.title: Debt, Work, and Integrity: Practical Wisdom for Kingdom Stewards
5.overview:
The Bible is remarkably practical about money. It addresses not just the theology of wealth but the everyday realities of debt, honest work, fair wages, contracts, and business practices. The Mosaic law had detailed provisions governing lending (no interest to fellow Israelites, Deut. 23:19-20), debt relief (the Sabbath year, Deut. 15:1-3), fair wages (Deut. 24:14-15), honest weights (Lev. 19:35-36), and honest dealing in commerce (Prov. 11:1). These were not peripheral regulations; they were expressions of a covenant community where economic relationships were governed by the character of God.

In the New Testament, the call to integrity extends to the workplace and the marketplace. Paul instructs slaves (workers) to serve 'as for the Lord and not for men' (Col. 3:23) -- which means the quality of our work is a form of worship. The teaching that 'the laborer deserves his wages' (1 Tim. 5:18; Luke 10:7) implies fair compensation as a matter of justice. And the warning against debt -- 'owe no one anything, except to love each other' (Rom. 13:8) -- is not an absolute prohibition of all borrowing but a serious caution against the bondage of debt.

This unit takes up the practical questions: How should a Christian approach debt? What does it mean to work with integrity? How do we handle contracts, taxes, and financial obligations? What does honest business practice look like? These are not small questions -- they are the arena where most of us live most of our financial lives. And Scripture has more wisdom for them than we usually realize.
5.theology: The ninth commandment ('You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor,' Exod. 20:16) extends, in the Reformed catechetical tradition, to all forms of commercial dishonesty. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q&A 144) lists as sins against this commandment 'prejudicing the truth, and the good name of our neighbors... by misconstruing intentions, words, and actions.' The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 110-111) addresses the eighth commandment ('You shall not steal') with remarkable breadth: it forbids all theft and fraud, 'whether by force or by seemingly legitimate means, such as false weights, deceptive advertising, counterfeit money, excessive interest, or any other means forbidden by God.' The Reformed tradition has always understood that economic life is moral life.
5.examples: A business owner reads Proverbs 11:1 ('A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight') and realizes she has been overstating her product's capabilities to close sales. She has never called it lying -- it's just 'marketing.' But the Proverb cuts through the euphemism. She begins to train her sales team in honest representation of their product, even when it costs a sale. Within two years, her customer retention rate has doubled. The integrity has built a reputation that marketing dollars never could. Honest business is also wise business -- though that is a byproduct, not the motive. The motive is that God hates false weights.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's instruction is not a prohibition of all borrowing (the OT law assumes lending and borrowing) but a call to honor financial obligations. The debts that remain unpaid dishonor both the lender and the God who commands us to keep our promises. The contrast -- owe nothing, but love everything -- is instructive: the only debt that is never discharged is the debt of love. We cannot love too much. We can borrow too much. The practical wisdom is to keep financial obligations clear and manageable, not allowing debt to create bondage that limits our freedom to serve God and others.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the most comprehensive theology of work in the New Testament: every task, no matter how mundane, performed 'as for the Lord.' Paul is speaking to slaves -- people with no career aspirations, no professional identity, no market freedom. And he says: even you are serving the Lord Christ. This transforms the workplace from an economic arena into a worship space. The quality of our work is a form of testimony. The integrity of our dealings is a form of proclamation. We are always, in every task, representing the one whose name we bear.

verseByVerse.quote: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs is blunt about debt: it creates a form of bondage. The wise person avoids unnecessary debt not out of fear but because freedom -- the freedom to give, to serve, to change direction, to respond to God's call -- is worth more than the things debt purchases. This is not a call to poverty; it is a call to financial freedom as a condition for kingdom availability. The person drowning in debt has limited options. The person with margin -- financial and emotional -- is available to God in ways that the indebted person simply cannot be.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights... I am the LORD your God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The phrase 'I am the LORD your God' appears throughout Leviticus as the foundation for every command. Here it is the foundation for honest weights and measures -- commercial integrity. God identifies himself with the honest transaction, the fair price, the accurate representation. To cheat in business is not merely to wrong your neighbor; it is to act contrary to the character of the God who has redeemed you. The marketplace is not a God-free zone. 'I am the LORD your God' -- including at the cash register, the contract table, and the salary negotiation.

6.title: Eternal Perspective: Laying Up Treasure in Heaven
6.overview:
Jesus' most concentrated teaching on money is found in the Sermon on the Mount, and its climax is this: 'Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also' (Matt. 6:19-21). This is not an economic strategy; it is a vision of reality. There are two kinds of treasure, two kinds of investment, two kinds of return -- and only one kind lasts.

The eternal perspective transforms our relationship to money by situating it in its proper context. Money is temporary -- at death, it all stays behind. Relationships, character, souls won for the kingdom, justice done, the poor served, the church built -- these endure. Randy Alcorn develops this with the image of an 'eternal investment portfolio': every act of generosity is a deposit into an account that compounds forever. Every dollar held tightly stays here; every dollar given in faith goes ahead.

This final unit draws together everything the study has covered and asks the question that Jesus himself asked: what is your treasure? Not what you say you value, but what you actually invest in, protect, worry about, and pursue. And it ends with the great hope: a new creation in which there is no poverty, no economic injustice, no anxiety about provision -- because God himself will be the provision, the treasure, the inheritance, the wealth of his people forever. 'The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it' (Rev. 21:24) -- the wealth of the nations, purified and transformed, offered to the glory of God in the new Jerusalem.
6.theology: The doctrine of new creation is the capstone of a Reformed theology of money. Because God will redeem the material world (not destroy it), the things we do in this world with our money -- the buildings we fund, the justice we pursue, the poor we serve, the gospel we finance -- are not lost at death but transformed. N.T. Wright develops this: whatever is done in the present in conformity with the kingdom of God will somehow be part of the renewed creation. This gives extraordinary weight to economic decisions made in faith. We are not just managing temporal assets; we are making deposits into the fabric of the new creation. The eschatological hope does not make present generosity less urgent; it makes it infinitely more meaningful.
6.examples: John Wesley famously said: 'Earn all you can, save all you can, give all you can.' He died with a few coins to his name -- everything else had been given away. He did not consider himself poor. He considered himself invested. A young couple, newly married, decide early in their marriage to set a 'lifestyle cap' -- a ceiling on their standard of living -- and to give away everything above it as their income grows. Twenty years later, as successful professionals, they are giving away the majority of their income. They report that this decision, made early and held consistently, has been the single greatest factor in their spiritual health and marital harmony. The treasure is in heaven. The heart has followed it there.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The command is not 'don't have things' but 'don't treasure things' -- don't deposit your heart in them, don't draw your security from them, don't define yourself by them. Jesus offers a binary: treasure on earth (temporary, perishable, vulnerable) or treasure in heaven (permanent, imperishable, secure). The choice is not just financial; it is directional. It determines where your heart ends up. And Jesus says the heart follows the treasure -- which means the most powerful way to change your heart is to change where you invest. Give, and your heart will follow to where you have given.

verseByVerse.quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail... For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's version of the treasure saying is preceded by a command: 'Sell your possessions and give to the needy.' Jesus is not recommending this as one option among many; he is describing the direction of the kingdom. The kingdom community holds possessions loosely enough to liquidate them for the sake of others. This is not universal poverty; it is universal generosity. The 'moneybags that do not grow old' are not a metaphor for feelings; they are a promise about the permanence of kingdom investment. What we give away in faith is kept by God forever.

verseByVerse.quote: They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul describes a divine economic exchange: the wealthy are to use their wealth to become 'rich in good works' -- which is the wealth that matters eternally. In doing so, they 'store up treasure for themselves' as a 'good foundation for the future.' This is not works-righteousness; it is kingdom investment. The outcome is breathtaking: 'that they may take hold of that which is truly life.' What is truly life? Not financial security, not comfort, not legacy -- but God himself, experienced fully in the new creation. All generosity is moving us toward that.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more...' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The end of the story is not prosperity; it is presence. The wealth of the new creation is God himself -- dwelling with his people, wiping every tear, making all things new. Every dollar given away in faith, every sacrifice made for the kingdom, every act of generosity toward the poor -- it all points here, to this moment, to this dwelling. We do not give to earn this; we give because we believe it. And when we believe it with our hearts and our wallets, we have truly understood what money is for: a temporary tool for eternal purposes, to be held loosely and given joyfully, until the day when we need nothing -- because we have everything, in him.
